Yellowfin goby Acanthogobius flavimanus attains a maximum recorded total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that positions it as one of the larger gobiid species inhabiting estuarine and coastal waters of the northwestern Pacific. Field surveys conducted across its native range from Japan to the Korean Peninsula indicate that this species typically matures at a markedly smaller body size; puberty is commonly observed when individuals reach a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters]. This substantial delay between the onset of sexual maturation and the achievement of asymptotic length suggests a prolonged period of continued somatic investment following reproductive activation, a life-history strategy shared with several other temperate gobies that occupy highly seasonal environments. The growth trajectory leading to the 30-centimeter ultimate length, which corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 193 grams [Wwi = approximately 193 grams], is characterized by rapid juvenile gains followed by a gradual deceleration as fish approach their terminal size. Comparative data from related species in the Gobiidae family further highlight that the relatively modest length at puberty relative to ultimate length represents an adaptive response to unpredictable spawning-season mortality.

Reproductive output in Yellowfin goby has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that maintain a stable water temperature of 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C], a thermal regime typical of its spring spawning season. Under these conditions, gravid females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that equates to approximately 101 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 101 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring at a frequency of approximately once per day [F_R_i = spawning occurring at a frequency of approximately once per day], a figure derived from direct observation of sequential spawning events over the breeding period. This daily fecundity reflects a spawning strategy that prioritizes numerous, relatively small clutches distributed across the reproductive season rather than a single large batch. The 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C] thermal environment was selected to match the thermal optimum for oocyte development and larval survival reported in the literature. The maximum recorded longevity for this species was also established under the same thermal conditions at 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C], with the oldest documented individual surviving approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years] in a monitored mesocosm population. This lifespan is consistent with the semelparous-to-weakly-iteroparous continuum seen in many coastal gobies.

The embryonic development of Acanthogobius flavimanus proceeds relatively slowly at cooler incubation temperatures. Eggs maintained at a constant 13 °C [T = 13 °C] require a developmental period of 28 days [ab = 28 days] before eclosion, a duration that reflects the reduced metabolic rates imposed by lower thermal regimes. Upon hatching at this temperature, the resulting yolk-sac larva emerges with an exceptionally small wet weight of just 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], a mass that underscores the highly altricial, endotrophic nature of the earliest free-living stage. This negligible initial biomass is derived from the modest dimensions of the fertilized egg, which typically measures approximately 5.5 millimeters in length and 0.9 millimeters in width. The 28-day incubation period at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] is markedly extended compared to the shorter durations reported for congeneric species spawning in warmer waters, suggesting that thermal variability across the species range can generate substantial variation in hatching phenology. The relationship between egg size and larval mass has been documented through both laboratory and field collections.

Following the transition to exogenous feeding, juvenile Yellowfin gobies undergo a rapid phase of mass gain that culminates in the attainment of puberty at a wet weight of approximately 24 grams [Wwp = approximately 24 grams]. This body mass corresponds closely to the 15-centimeter total length threshold (15 centimeters) [Lp = 15 centimeters] at which gonadal recrudescence is first observed histologically. The energetic investment required to reach this relatively modest pubertal mass is comparatively low, enabling individuals to enter the reproductive population within their first year even under suboptimal foraging conditions. In contrast, the 193-gram ultimate wet weight (193 grams) [Wwi = 193 grams] represents a more than eightfold increase in biomass from the pubertal stage, indicating substantial post-maturational growth. Field-caught specimens exceeding 25 centimeters in total length are almost invariably reproductively active females, suggesting that the largest individuals allocate considerable resources to iteroparous spawning across multiple seasons. The allometric relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical cubic scaling pattern, with the 24-gram (24 grams) [Wwp = 24 grams] and 193-gram (193 grams) [Wwi = 193 grams] values reflecting the expected power-law increase.

The life history of the Yellowfin goby exhibits a clear thermal dependency that integrates the species' reproductive and survival strategies. The maximum daily spawning rate of approximately 101 eggs per event [N_R_i = approximately 101 eggs per event] was recorded exclusively at 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C], a temperature that simultaneously governs the maximum lifespan of approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years] under identical thermal conditions. This coupling of high reproductive output with a relatively short maximum lifespan suggests a life-history trade-off in which early and intense spawning effort is prioritized over extended somatic persistence. Conversely, the 28-day incubation period observed at the cooler temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] produces larvae weighing only 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], demonstrating that thermal conditions during early development directly influence initial larval quality. Populations inhabiting more thermally variable estuaries may experience substantial interannual variation in both hatching success and eventual recruitment. A comparative analysis across Gobiidae indicates that the species' moderate size at puberty and high fecundity align it with an opportunistic life-history strategy well suited to dynamic coastal environments.
